sourceReview: Read bundled BSB Psalm 87 in full with each verse's related passages before drafting. References are thematic or literary comparisons, not an invented historical occasion. Scripture is never stored in the notes; it loads from the bundled BSB.

study.title: Born in Zion
study.intro: A short, surprising song of the sons of Korah celebrates Zion, the city God founded and loves, and then imagines former enemy nations being registered as her native-born citizens, all finding their springs of joy in her.
study.context: Psalm 87 is headed 'A Psalm of the sons of Korah. A song.' It is compact and almost abrupt in style. Verses 1-3 praise Zion as the city God founded and loves. Verses 4-6 picture God Himself enrolling foreign peoples, including old oppressors, as citizens born in Zion. Verse 7 ends with music and joy. The psalm anticipates the promise to Abraham that all nations would be blessed, and the New Testament picture of a heavenly Jerusalem whose citizens come from every people.
study.peopleNote: The heading credits the sons of Korah, the Levite family of temple singers, so they are linked. Verse 2 mentions the dwellings of Jacob, so Jacob is linked. The welcome of the nations into God's city is fulfilled through Jesus, so He is linked. God is never portrayed as a human body in planned art.

verses.title: Founded on holy mountains
verses.heading: The city whose foundation God laid
verses.meaning: The song opens mid-thought: 'He has founded His city on the holy mountains.' The 'He' is the LORD, named in the next verse. Zion's security does not rest on its walls, its kings or its location, but on the fact that God Himself laid its foundation. The plural 'holy mountains' may describe the hills around Jerusalem. Whatever stands on God's foundation stands firm when other cities fall.
verses.context: Psalm 48:1-2 praises Mount Zion as beautiful in elevation, the joy of the whole earth. Isaiah 28:16 speaks of God laying in Zion a tested and precious cornerstone. Hebrews 11:10 says Abraham looked for the city with foundations whose architect and builder is God.
explore: Sons of Korah
Levite descendants of Korah who served as temple singers and gatekeepers and wrote several psalms.
Zion
The hill in Jerusalem where the temple stood, and by extension the city and people where God chose to dwell.
verses.reflect: What in your life is built on something God laid down, and what is resting on your own effort alone?
verses.alt: A walled hilltop city of stone stands above terraced slopes at dawn.

verses.title: Loved gates
verses.heading: Why God prizes Zion above Jacob's homes
verses.meaning: Verse 2 says, 'The LORD loves the gates of Zion more than all the dwellings of Jacob.' This is not contempt for ordinary homes across Israel. The gates stand for the whole city, and Zion was the place God chose for His name, His temple and His worship. God's love for the city is the love of choice, not of merit. It was where heaven and earth met, so it mattered more than any single town or household.
verses.context: Deuteronomy 12:5 told Israel to seek the place the LORD would choose to put His name. Psalm 78:68 says He chose Mount Zion, which He loved. Psalm 132:13-14 says the LORD has chosen Zion as His resting place forever.
explore: Gates
City entrances where trade, law cases and public gatherings happened, often standing for the whole city.
Jacob
The patriarch whose name stands for the whole nation of Israel descended from his twelve sons.
verses.reflect: Where do you meet with God most consistently, and how could you treasure that place or habit more?
verses.alt: Tall wooden city gates stand open with people passing through in morning light.

verses.title: Glorious things spoken
verses.heading: A reputation given by God
verses.meaning: 'Glorious things are ascribed to you, O city of God.' The singer turns to address the city directly. The glorious things are not boasting about architecture but the promises God had spoken about Zion through His prophets: that He would dwell there, defend it and draw the nations to it. The 'Selah' invites a pause before the most startling of those glorious things is announced in the next verse.
verses.context: Isaiah 2:2-3 promises that many peoples will stream to the mountain of the LORD's house. Isaiah 60:14 says Zion will be called the City of the LORD. The hymn 'Glorious Things of Thee Are Spoken' is based on this verse.
explore: City of God
A title for Jerusalem as the place of God's presence, later used for His people and the heavenly city.
Selah
A musical or liturgical marker of uncertain meaning, often understood as a pause for reflection.
verses.reflect: Which promise God has spoken over His people do you most need to remember today?
verses.alt: A scroll lies open on a stone ledge overlooking a hilltop city.

verses.title: Enemies enrolled
verses.heading: Former foes who now know the LORD
verses.meaning: Here God speaks: 'I will mention Rahab and Babylon among those who know Me, along with Philistia, Tyre, and Cush, when I say, This one was born in Zion.' Rahab is a poetic name for Egypt. These were Israel's oppressors, rivals and distant neighbors. Yet God says they will 'know Me' and be counted as native-born citizens of His city. This is not conquest but adoption, grace reaching to the very nations that had been enemies.
verses.context: Isaiah 19:24-25 promises that Egypt and Assyria will one day be blessed alongside Israel. Genesis 12:3 promised that all families of the earth would be blessed through Abraham. Ephesians 2:19 says believing Gentiles are no longer strangers but fellow citizens.
explore: Rahab
Here a poetic name for Egypt, meaning proud or arrogant, not the woman of Jericho in Joshua 2.
Cush
The land south of Egypt along the upper Nile, roughly ancient Nubia, often seen as the far edge of the world.
verses.reflect: Is there a person or group you find hard to imagine as part of God's family? How does this verse challenge you?
verses.alt: People in varied clothing from many lands walk together on a road toward a hill city.

verses.title: This one and that one
verses.heading: Every citizen established by the Most High
verses.meaning: Verse 5 widens the picture: 'This one and that one were born in her, and the Most High Himself will establish her.' The repeated 'this one and that one' stresses individuals, not just nations in bulk. Each person is known and counted. The city's growth does not depend on human recruitment or strength; 'the Most High Himself' secures it. Belonging to God's people is a birth He grants, not a status we earn.
verses.context: John 3:3 says no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again. Galatians 4:26 calls the Jerusalem above 'our mother.' Philippians 3:20 says our citizenship is in heaven.
explore: Most High
A title of God stressing His supreme rule over every nation and power.
Establish
To make firm and secure so that it lasts, as a builder sets a foundation that will not shift.
verses.reflect: How does it change your sense of belonging to know God counts you individually as born into His city?
verses.alt: Two strangers greet each other warmly inside a stone city gate.

verses.title: The register of peoples
verses.heading: God writes the names Himself
verses.meaning: 'The LORD will record in the register of the peoples: This one was born in Zion.' The picture is of a census roll kept by God. In the ancient world your birthplace defined your rights and identity. Here God personally enters the names of people from every nation as Zion-born. No one sneaks in, and no one is left off by mistake. The 'Selah' asks us to pause over the wonder of our names in His book.
verses.context: Exodus 32:32 mentions God's book where names are written. Luke 10:20 tells the disciples to rejoice that their names are written in heaven. Revelation 21:27 says only those written in the Lamb's book of life enter the city.
explore: Register
An official list of citizens or family records, like the genealogies kept in Ezra and Nehemiah.
Born in Zion
Counted as a full native citizen of God's city, with every right of belonging, regardless of origin.
verses.reflect: Take a moment to rejoice that, through Jesus, your name can be written in God's book. What does that free you from?
verses.alt: A large bound ledger lies open on a wooden table beside an ink pot and reed pen.

verses.title: Springs of joy
verses.heading: Music from those who belong
verses.meaning: The psalm ends with celebration: 'Singers and pipers will proclaim, All my springs of joy are in You.' Those newly counted as Zion's citizens join the music. 'Springs' pictures fresh water rising up, the source of life in a dry land. The 'You' is the city as the place of God's presence, and ultimately God Himself. Every true joy for every nation flows from Him, not from where we came from.
verses.context: Psalm 46:4 speaks of a river whose streams make glad the city of God. Isaiah 12:3 says, 'With joy you will draw water from the springs of salvation.' John 7:37-38 records Jesus promising streams of living water to all who come to Him.
explore: Pipers
Players of reed flutes or pipes, used at festivals, processions and celebrations in Israel.
Springs
Natural sources of fresh water, precious in a dry land and a picture of life that comes from God.
verses.reflect: Where are you looking for joy right now? What would it look like to say to God, 'All my springs are in You'?
verses.alt: Musicians with flutes and lyres play beside a flowing spring at the foot of a hill.
